big: Rohan buys a ₹1 lakh gold necklace and, after a year, finds the jeweller will buy it back for only ₹88,000. The gold did not fall. The costs of buying and selling took the rest.

lines: Gold is gold. Why the big difference between buying and selling?
On jewellery you pay making charges that are not recovered, and a jeweller buys back at a lower price. Check purity too. A hallmark is your proof.

rows: Buyback offer, gold value less a cut
note: These numbers are made up to show the idea. Making charges and the buyback gap vary by jeweller and design.

q: Meena buys gold jewellery. How can she check its purity?
opts: Trust the lighting in the shop
Ask a stranger who passes by
Weigh it on her own scale at home
why: Lighting makes jewellery look shiny, and proves no purity.
A stranger outside has no way to certify purity.
The hallmark with its HUID shows purity under BIS.
Weight shows how much it weighs, not how pure it is.

q: A ring is marked 22 carat. What does that mean?
opts: It is not gold at all
why: 22 carat is about 91.6% gold, mixed with other metals.
Almost pure gold is 24 carat, and not 22 carat.
22 carat is far above half gold in content.
A 22 carat ring is largely made of gold.

q: Rohan sells the necklace he bought a year ago. Which cost is usually not recovered?
why: The weight is valued at the day's price when sold.
A hallmark is a mark of purity, not a cost to him.
Memory is not a cost on a bill, so it is wrong.
Making charges pay for crafting and are not recovered.

opts: A fee paid to SEBI on every sale made
Gap between buying and buyback prices
The premium on a policy for gold
why: SEBI does not charge a fee on gold jewellery.
It is the gap between what you pay and what you get back.
A premium belongs to insurance, not to gold buyback.
A subsidy is a government payment, unrelated to this gap.

pts: Check the BIS hallmark and HUID before buying jewellery.
Making charges and the buyback gap are real costs.
